code.title: Strings do not change: copy to edit, use a builder to build
code.python:
s = "hello"
# upper() cannot change s; it returns a brand new string
t = s.upper()
print("original: " + s)
print("upper copy: " + t)
print("original after: " + s)

# To edit one letter: copy into a list, change it, join into a new string
arr = list(s)
arr[0] = "j"
print("edited via char array: " + "".join(arr))

# To build a long string, collect the pieces in a list and join once
parts = []
for i in range(10):
    parts.append(str(i))
print("built: " + "".join(parts))
# Time O(N) and space O(N) for a result of N characters

followUps:
The map would lose the entry even though it is still inside. A HashMap picks a bucket from the key's hash at the moment you call put. If the key's letters changed later, its hash would change too, so get would look in a different bucket and find nothing.

Example: key "cat" is stored in bucket 3. The key is changed to "car", which hashes to bucket 7. get("car") searches bucket 7 and returns null. get("cat") searches bucket 3, finds the entry, but equals fails because the stored key now reads "car". The value can never be reached again, and it also cannot be removed, so it leaks memory.

Put the characters in something that can change, edit there, and turn it back into a String once at the end. Use StringBuilder when you add or remove text, and a char[] when the length stays the same (swap, reverse, replace a letter).

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(n);
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sb.append(words[i]);
String result = sb.toString();   // one copy at the end

With s += x in a loop, every step copies everything written so far: for 1,000 one-letter appends that is 1 + 2 + … + 1,000 = 500,500 character copies. The builder does about 2,000. Cost: O(N) time and O(N) space instead of O(N2) time.

code.title: Same letters is not the same object: content check, identity check, intern
code.python:
import sys

a = "hello"                    # literal
b = "".join(["hel", "lo"])     # built at run time: a new object
print("a = " + a + ", b = " + b)

# == in Python compares the letters (like equals in Java)
print("same content: " + str(a == b).lower())

# "is" asks "is this the very same object?" (like == in Java)
print("same object: " + str(a is b).lower())

# sys.intern returns the one shared copy kept by the interpreter
a2 = sys.intern(a)
c = sys.intern(b)
print("same object after intern: " + str(a2 is c).lower())
# == costs O(N) time for N letters; "is" costs O(1); space O(1)

followUps:
intern() gives you the one shared copy of a string that the JVM keeps in its string pool. If a string with the same letters is already in the pool, you get that object back; if not, yours is added and returned. After interning, two strings with equal letters are the same object, so == is true.

It is useful when the same few texts repeat many times. Example: a file with 1,000,000 rows and only 50 different city names. Without interning you may hold 1,000,000 separate String objects; with it you hold 50. The price is a pool lookup that costs O(length) per call, so do not intern strings that are all different. Still compare with equals; intern is a memory tool, not a comparison style.

Yes. A char is a primitive value, really just a small number, so == compares the two numbers directly. s.charAt(0) == 'a' is correct and costs O(1).

Example: 'a' is 97 and 'A' is 65, so 'a' == 'A' is false and 'a' == 97 is true. Two things to watch: (1) the check is case-sensitive, so lowercase first if case should not matter; (2) the boxed type Character is an object, so == on two Character variables compares references and is only reliable for cached values up to 127. Use equals or unbox to char in that case, for example when reading from a List<Character>.

code.title: Letter counts: 26-slot array against a hash map (anagram check)
code.python:
s, t = "listen", "silent"
print("s = " + s + ", t = " + t)

# 26-slot list: slot 0 is 'a', slot 25 is 'z'
cs = [0] * 26
ct = [0] * 26
for c in s:
    cs[ord(c) - ord("a")] += 1
for c in t:
    ct[ord(c) - ord("a")] += 1
line = "counts of s:"
for i in range(26):
    if cs[i] > 0:
        line += " " + chr(ord("a") + i) + "=" + str(cs[i])
print(line)
# Comparing two count lists is always 26 steps
print("anagram (26-slot array): " + str(cs == ct).lower())

# Hash map (dict): works for any character, but is slower per step
m = {}
for c in s:
    m[c] = m.get(c, 0) + 1
for c in t:
    m[c] = m.get(c, 0) - 1
ok = all(v == 0 for v in m.values())
print("anagram (hash map): " + str(ok).lower())
# Time O(N); space O(1) for the list, O(distinct characters) for the dict

followUps:
Keep one number, matches, that says how many of the 26 letters currently have the same count in the window and in the target. The window is an anagram exactly when matches == 26, so each slide costs O(1) instead of 26 comparisons.

// add letter x to the window
if (win[x] == need[x]) matches--;   // it was equal, now it is not
win[x]++;
if (win[x] == need[x]) matches++;   // it became equal
// removing a letter is the same with win[x]--

Example: target "ab", text "cba". Window "cb" has matches = 23 (a, b and c differ). Slide: add 'a', remove 'c' gives "ba" and matches = 26, so index 1 is a hit. Time O(N), space O(1). Simply comparing all 26 slots at every step is also O(N), just 26 times more work.

The index c - 'a' goes out of the 0 to 25 range, because uppercase letters have smaller codes than lowercase ones. For example 'A' - 'a' is 65 − 97 = −32.

What happens next depends on the language: Java and C# throw an index-out-of-bounds exception, Python raises IndexError for −32 (but for small negatives it silently counts from the end of the list), JavaScript quietly creates a property named "-32" and your counts are wrong, and C++ writes outside the array, which is undefined behaviour.

Fixes: lowercase the input first if case should not matter; use 52 slots or a 128-slot ASCII array if 'A' and 'a' are different letters; use a hash map when the alphabet is unknown. Always ask the interviewer which characters can appear.

code.title: Counting copies: grow by doubling against grow by +10
code.python:
# Simulates n appends into a growing array and counts copied characters
def copies(n, doubling):
    cap = 1 if doubling else 10
    size = 0
    copied = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        if size == cap:            # full: move everything to a bigger array
            copied += size
            cap = cap * 2 if doubling else cap + 10
        size += 1                  # the append itself: one write
    return copied

n = 1000
print("appends: " + str(n))
a = copies(n, True)
b = copies(n, False)
# Doubling: copies are 1 + 2 + 4 + ... which stays below 2N
print("doubling: copies = " + str(a) + ", total work = " + str(a + n))
# +10: copies are 10 + 20 + 30 + ... which grows like N*N/20
print("grow by +10: copies = " + str(b) + ", total work = " + str(b + n))
# Doubling: O(N) total, O(1) amortized per append. +10: O(N^2) total. Space O(N).

followUps:
Appending would become slow: O(N) per append on average and O(N2) for the whole job. With a fixed step the array fills up again after every 10 appends, so a full copy happens N/10 times, and the copies keep getting longer.

Count it for N = 1,000: the copies are 10 + 20 + 30 + … + 990 = 49,500 characters. With doubling they are 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 512 = 1,023. For N = 1,000,000 the gap is about 50 billion against about 1 million.

The reason doubling works is that each copy "pays" for as many cheap appends as it moved. A fixed step never earns that: the copy grows with N but only 10 cheap appends follow it. Any constant factor above 1 (×1.5, ×2) gives amortized O(1); any constant addition does not.

Anything that touches the front or the middle, or that reads the whole content, costs O(N): insert(0, x), deleteCharAt(0), delete(i, j), replace, reverse(), indexOf and toString(). Inside a loop of N steps each of these makes the total O(N2).

Only work at the end is cheap: append, charAt, setCharAt, length, and setLength(len − 1) to remove the last character.

Example: building a reversed string with sb.insert(0, c) shifts everything on each step, 0 + 1 + … + 999 = 499,500 moves for 1,000 letters. Do 1,000 appends and one reverse() at the end: about 2,000 steps. Also call toString() once after the loop, not in the loop condition.

code.title: Longest palindromic substring: expand around each center
code.python:
# Grows outwards from (l, r) while the two ends match; returns the length found
def expand(s, l, r):
    while l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]:
        l -= 1
        r += 1
    return r - l - 1   # l and r stopped one step outside the palindrome

s = "forgeeksskeegfor"
start, best = 0, 0
for c in range(len(s)):
    odd = expand(s, c, c)        # center is the letter c
    even = expand(s, c, c + 1)   # center is the gap after c
    length = max(odd, even)
    if length > best:
        best = length
        start = c - (length - 1) // 2   # works for odd and even lengths
print("s = " + s)
print("longest palindrome: " + s[start:start + best] + " (length " + str(best) + ")")
# Time O(N^2): 2N-1 centers, each can expand up to N. Space O(1).

followUps:
Use the same expand-around-center loop, but add 1 to a counter every time the two ends match. Each successful step of the expansion is one more palindrome with that center.

  1. For every index c, expand from (c, c) for odd lengths and from (c, c + 1) for even lengths.
  2. While s[l] == s[r]: count++, then l−−, r++.
int count = 0;
for (int c = 0; c < n; c++)
  for (int k = 0; k < 2; k++) {          // k = 0 odd, k = 1 even
    int l = c, r = c + k;
    while (l >= 0 && r < n && s.charAt(l--) == s.charAt(r++)) count++;
  }

Example "aaa": centers give a, a, a, aa, aa, aaa, so the answer is 6. Time O(N2), space O(1). Manacher's radius array gives the same count in O(N).

Manacher finds the longest palindrome around every center in one left-to-right pass, O(N) in total, by reusing what it already knows. It remembers the palindrome that reaches furthest to the right; a new center inside it copies the answer of its mirror position on the other side (cut off at the right edge) and only compares characters beyond that edge.

Because every real comparison pushes the right edge forward and the edge never moves back, there are at most about 2N comparisons. Putting # between letters ("aba" becomes "#a#b#a#") makes every palindrome odd-length, so one loop handles both cases. Example: in "#a#b#a#" the center 'b' has radius 3, which is the length of "aba". Space O(N).

code.title: Rabin-Karp: slide a rolling hash over the text
code.python:
txt, pat = "abracadabra", "abra"
B, M = 31, 1_000_000_007
n, m = len(txt), len(pat)

def val(c):
    return ord(c) - ord("a") + 1          # letters are 1..26, never 0

power = pow(B, m - 1, M)                  # weight of the leftmost letter
hp = hw = 0                               # hash of pattern, hash of current window
for i in range(m):
    hp = (hp * B + val(pat[i])) % M
    hw = (hw * B + val(txt[i])) % M

found = []
for i in range(n - m + 1):
    # equal hashes: check the letters to rule out a collision
    if hw == hp and txt[i:i + m] == pat:
        found.append(i)
    if i + m < n:
        out = val(txt[i]) * power % M
        hw = ((hw - out + M) % M * B + val(txt[i + m])) % M   # O(1) slide

print("text = " + txt + ", pattern = " + pat)
print("pattern hash = " + str(hp))
print("matches at: [" + ", ".join(str(x) for x in found) + "]")
# Expected time O(N + M), worst case O(N*M) with many collisions. Space O(1).

followUps:
Because a letter worth 0 adds nothing to the hash, so strings that differ only by that letter get the same hash. It is the same as leading zeros in a number: 007 and 7 are equal.

Example with base 31 and 'a' = 0: "a" = 0, "aa" = 0·31 + 0 = 0, "aaa" = 0, and "ab" = 0·31 + 1 = 1 = "b". All these different strings collide every time, whatever modulus you pick. With 'a' = 1: "a" = 1, "aa" = 1·31 + 1 = 32, "ab" = 33, "b" = 2, all different.

So map letters to 1..26 with c - 'a' + 1 (or use the raw character code, which is never 0 for real text), and choose a base larger than the largest letter value.

Add the modulus back before taking the remainder again, so the value is never below zero. In Java, C++, C# and JavaScript, % keeps the sign of the left side, so a negative number stays negative and no longer equals the hash you compare it with.

long out = val(s[i]) * power % M;        // already in 0..M-1
h = (h - out + M) % M;                   // now in 0..M-1 again
h = (h * B + val(s[i + m])) % M;

Example with M = 101: h = 5, out = 20. 5 − 20 = −15, and −15 % 101 is −15 in Java. Adding M first gives (5 − 20 + 101) % 101 = 86, which is the right answer. Python's % returns 86 by itself, but the + M form is harmless there too. Adding M once is enough only when both numbers are already reduced to 0..M−1.

code.title: Collisions: one small hash against two hashes together

followUps:
Because anyone who knows your base and modulus can prepare, in advance, many different strings that all have the same hash, and then send them to you. A hash is only "random" to someone who cannot predict it.

What goes wrong: if you trust equal hashes without checking letters, you return wrong answers (a hacked solution on a judge). If you do check letters, every window becomes a false alarm that costs a full comparison, so O(N + M) turns into O(N·M); in a hash table all keys land in one bucket and each lookup becomes O(N). On a web service this is a denial-of-service attack called hash flooding.

Fix: pick the base at random when the program starts, for example B = 256 + random.nextInt(1_000_000). The attacker's prepared strings then collide only with the usual tiny probability.

Combine them into one 64-bit number: key = h1 * M2 + h2, where M2 is the modulus of the second hash. Since h2 is always below M2, every pair (h1, h2) gives a different key, like writing a two-digit number in base M2.

long key = h1 * M2 + h2;        // or (h1 << 32) | h2 if both fit in 32 bits
map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum);

Example: h1 = 5, h2 = 7, M2 = 1,000,000,009 gives 5,000,000,052. With both moduli near 109 the key stays below 1018, which fits in a long. This is faster than a string key like "5,7" or a pair object, because no extra object is created. In JavaScript a Number is exact only up to 253, so use a BigInt or a string key there.

code.title: Build the LPS array in O(M)
code.python:
def build_lps(pat):
    m = len(pat)
    lps = [0] * m              # lps[0] is always 0
    length, i = 0, 1           # length = length of the current border
    while i < m:
        if pat[i] == pat[length]:
            length += 1        # the border grows by one letter
            lps[i] = length
            i += 1
        elif length > 0:
            length = lps[length - 1]   # try the next shorter border, i stays
        else:
            lps[i] = 0         # no border ends here
            i += 1
    return lps

pat = "aabaaab"
print("pattern = " + pat)
print("lps = [" + ", ".join(str(x) for x in build_lps(pat)) + "]")
# Time O(M): length rises at most M times, and each fallback lowers it. Space O(M).

followUps:
The answer is [0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3]. Here is each step, with len = the border length carried in:

ipat[i]what happenslps[i]
0aalways 00
1aequals pat[0], len = 11
2bdiffers from pat[1]; fall back to len = lps[0] = 0; differs from pat[0]0
3aequals pat[0], len = 11
4aequals pat[1], len = 22
5adiffers from pat[2] = b; fall back to len = lps[1] = 1; equals pat[1], len = 22
6bequals pat[2], len = 33

Check the last one: "aabaaab" starts with "aab" and ends with "aab".

Because len is a length, and a matched prefix of length len occupies indexes 0 to len − 1. Its last index is len − 1, so the next shorter border of that matched part is stored in lps[len − 1].

lps[len] describes the prefix that also includes pat[len], the very character that just failed to match. That character is not part of what we matched, so its entry answers a different question.

Example "aabaaab" at i = 5: len = 2 (we matched "aa"), and pat[5] = 'a' differs from pat[2] = 'b'. Correct: len = lps[1] = 1, then pat[5] equals pat[1], so lps[5] = 2. Wrong: len = lps[2] = 0, then pat[5] equals pat[0], giving lps[5] = 1 and missing the border "aa".

code.title: KMP search with a step counter: never more than 2N loop steps
code.python:
txt, pat = "abababcabababab", "abab"
n, m = len(txt), len(pat)

lps = [0] * m
i, length = 1, 0
while i < m:                           # build the LPS table
    if pat[i] == pat[length]:
        length += 1
        lps[i] = length
        i += 1
    elif length > 0:
        length = lps[length - 1]
    else:
        i += 1

found = []
i = j = steps = 0
while i < n:
    steps += 1                         # one loop step
    if txt[i] == pat[j]:
        i += 1                         # both pointers move forward
        j += 1
        if j == m:
            found.append(i - m)
            j = lps[j - 1]             # keep the overlap for the next match
    elif j > 0:
        j = lps[j - 1]                 # j falls back, i does not move
    else:
        i += 1                         # nothing matched, move on

print("text = " + txt + ", pattern = " + pat)
print("matches at: [" + ", ".join(str(x) for x in found) + "]")
print("loop steps: " + str(steps) + " (limit 2N = " + str(2 * n) + ")")
# Time O(N + M), space O(M) for the LPS table

followUps:
No, never. On a mismatch only the pattern pointer j falls back; the text pointer i stays where it is and the same text character is compared again with an earlier pattern character.

Example: text "aaab", pattern "aab" (lps = [0, 1, 0]). At i = 2, j = 2 we compare 'a' with 'b' and fail. KMP sets j = lps[1] = 1 and keeps i = 2. Now text[2] = 'a' equals pat[1] = 'a', so i = 3, j = 2, then 'b' equals 'b' and we report a match at index 1. The naive method would have moved i back to 1.

This is why KMP works on a stream: you can read characters from a socket or a huge file one at a time and never keep or re-read old ones. Memory is O(M) for the pattern and its table only.

After reporting a match, do not reset j to 0; set j = lps[m − 1]. That keeps the longest part of the match that can also be the beginning of the next match, so matches that overlap are found.

if (j == m) {
    result.add(i - m);     // match starts here
    j = lps[j - 1];        // not j = 0
}

Example: text "aaaa", pattern "aa", lps = [0, 1]. With j = lps[1] = 1 the matches are at 0, 1 and 2. With j = 0 you only get 0 and 2, because the search restarts after the whole match. The cost stays O(N + M): this is just one more fallback of j, which the usual proof already counts. If the task wants non-overlapping matches, j = 0 is the correct choice.

code.title: Z-array with the [L, R) box, used for pattern search
code.python:
def z_array(s):
    n = len(s)
    z = [0] * n
    l = r = 0                          # box: s[l..r-1] equals a prefix of s
    for i in range(1, n):
        # inside the box: copy the mirror value, but not past the box edge
        if i < r:
            z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l])
        # extend with real comparisons
        while i + z[i] < n and s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]:
            z[i] += 1
        # this match reaches further right: it becomes the new box
        if i + z[i] > r:
            l, r = i, i + z[i]
    return z

pat, txt = "aab", "baabaaab"
s = pat + "$" + txt                    # '$' appears in neither string
z = z_array(s)
found = [i - len(pat) - 1 for i in range(len(pat) + 1, len(s)) if z[i] == len(pat)]
print("s = " + s)
print("z = [" + ", ".join(str(x) for x in z) + "]")
print("matches in text at: [" + ", ".join(str(x) for x in found) + "]")
# Time O(N + M): every successful comparison moves r to the right. Space O(N + M).

followUps:
Because the box only tells us what the characters up to R look like; past R we have not read anything yet. The mirror position's value may describe a match that runs further than the part of the box that is left, and we are not allowed to assume that extra part.

Example: s = "aaaab". Z[1] = 3 ("aaa" matches, then 'b' differs from 'a'), so the box is [1, 3]. For i = 2 the mirror is i − L = 1 with Z[1] = 3, but only R − i + 1 = 2 characters of the box remain. The true Z[2] is 2: s[4] = 'b' does not equal s[2] = 'a'. Copying 3 without the cap would be wrong.

So we take min(R − i + 1, Z[i − L]) as a safe starting value and let the comparison loop continue from R + 1. That loop is also what keeps the total work O(N).

Leave the separator out and add one extra condition. Compute Z on pat + txt directly, and report a match at text index i − m whenever i ≥ m and Z[i] ≥ m (not "equals m").

Why it is still correct: Z[i] ≥ m means the m characters starting at i equal the first m characters of the string, and those are exactly the pattern. Without a separator the value can run past m into the text, which is why the test becomes "at least m".

Example: pat = "aa", txt = "aaa", s = "aaaaa", Z = [0, 4, 3, 2, 1]. For i = 2, 3 the value is ≥ 2, so matches are at text indexes 0 and 1; i = 4 has Z = 1, no match. Other options: use KMP, which needs no separator at all, or work on an int array and use −1 as the separator. Cost is unchanged: O(N + M) time and space.

code.title: Where Rabin-Karp wins: several equal-length patterns in one pass
code.python:
B, M = 31, 1_000_000_007

def val(c):
    return ord(c) - ord("a") + 1

def poly_hash(s):
    h = 0
    for c in s:
        h = (h * B + val(c)) % M
    return h

txt = "abracadabra"
pats = ["abr", "cad", "dab"]
n, m = len(txt), 3
# One dict entry per pattern: a window is checked against all of them in O(1)
by_hash = {poly_hash(p): p for p in pats}
power = pow(B, m - 1, M)
print("text = " + txt + ", patterns = " + " ".join(pats))
hw = poly_hash(txt[:m])
for i in range(n - m + 1):
    p = by_hash.get(hw)
    # verify the letters so that a collision cannot give a wrong report
    if p is not None and txt[i:i + m] == p:
        print(str(i) + ": " + p)
    if i + m < n:                      # slide the window by one letter
        out = val(txt[i]) * power % M
        hw = ((hw - out + M) % M * B + val(txt[i + m])) % M
# Expected time O(N + K*m) for K patterns of length m; space O(K).
# KMP or Z would need one full pass over the text per pattern: O(K*N).

followUps:
Aho–Corasick, which is KMP extended from one pattern to a whole dictionary. Running KMP once per pattern costs O(K·N) for K patterns; Aho–Corasick reads the text only once.

How it works: put all patterns into a trie, then give every node a "failure link" to the longest proper suffix of its path that is also a path in the trie (the same idea as the LPS fallback). While scanning, follow a child on a match and a failure link on a mismatch; the text pointer never moves back.

Example: patterns {he, she, his, hers}, text "ushers". One pass reports "she" and "he" ending at index 3 and "hers" ending at index 5. Cost: O(total pattern length) to build, O(N + number of matches) to search. If all patterns have the same length, Rabin-Karp with a hash set is a simpler choice.

None of the three. Java's String.indexOf uses the simple method: find the next place where the first character matches, then compare the rest of the pattern one character at a time. Its worst case is O(N·M), with O(1) extra space.

It is still the right default, because on ordinary text a wrong start fails after one or two characters, so it behaves like O(N), and the JVM replaces the loop with very fast machine instructions. There is also no table to build, which matters for short patterns.

It only hurts on repetitive input. Example: text of 100,000 'a' characters and pattern of 50,000 'a' followed by 'b' needs about 50,000 × 50,000 = 2.5 billion comparisons. If the input can be chosen by an attacker or the limits are large, write KMP or Z yourself and say so in the interview.

code.title: Rotation check: search goal inside s + s with KMP

followUps:
Use the "minimal representation" two-pointer method (Booth's algorithm solves the same task): it finds the start index of the smallest rotation in O(N) time and O(1) space, without building or sorting the N rotations.

  1. Keep two candidate starts i = 0, j = 1 and k = number of letters on which they agree so far.
  2. Compare s[(i+k)%n] with s[(j+k)%n]. Equal: k++.
  3. Different: the candidate with the larger letter loses, and so do the k starts after it, so jump it forward by k + 1 and reset k.
int i = 0, j = 1, k = 0;
while (i < n && j < n && k < n) {
  int d = s.charAt((i+k)%n) - s.charAt((j+k)%n);
  if (d == 0) { k++; continue; }
  if (d > 0) i += k + 1; else j += k + 1;
  if (i == j) j++;  k = 0; }   // answer starts at Math.min(i, j)

Example "bca": the result is index 2, rotation "abc".

The position where goal is found inside s + s is the number of left shifts, so use a search that returns an index instead of only true or false.

Example: s = "waterbottle", goal = "erbottlewat". In "waterbottlewaterbottle" the goal starts at index 3, so moving the first 3 letters ("wat") to the end turns s into goal: 3 left shifts. The same result as right shifts is n − k = 11 − 3 = 8.

Two details: (1) KMP returns the first match, which is the smallest shift; a repeating string has more than one answer, for example "abab" matches itself at shifts 0 and 2. (2) Search only start positions 0 to n − 1, because index n is the same rotation as index 0. Cost stays O(N) time and O(N) space.

code.title: Near-duplicate check: word shingles and Jaccard similarity
code.python:
# All runs of k words in a row ("shingles"), kept as a set
def shingles(doc, k):
    w = doc.split(" ")
    return {" ".join(w[i:i + k]) for i in range(len(w) - k + 1)}

a = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
b = "the quick brown fox leaps over the lazy dog"
k = 3
sa, sb = shingles(a, k), shingles(b, k)
# shared = shingles that appear in both documents
shared = sum(1 for x in sa if x in sb)
total = len(sa) + len(sb) - shared     # size of the union
print("A: " + a)
print("B: " + b)
print("k = " + str(k) + ", shingles in A = " + str(len(sa)) + ", in B = " + str(len(sb)))
# Jaccard similarity = shared / total; close to 1 means near-duplicate
print("shared = " + str(shared) + ", total = " + str(total)
      + ", Jaccard = " + str(shared) + "/" + str(total))
# Time O(L * k) here; a rolling hash makes it O(L). Space O(L).
# Real systems store a 64-bit hash of each shingle, not the text.

followUps:
Pick k large enough that a shingle rarely appears in two unrelated documents by chance, and small enough that a small edit does not destroy most shingles. Then tune it on pairs that people have labelled as duplicate or not.

Too small: with k = 1 word, every English page shares "the", "of", "and", so everything looks similar. Too large: with k = 50 words, changing one word ruins up to 50 shingles, so a lightly edited copy looks different.

Common starting points are 3 to 5 words for web pages and news, or character shingles of about 5 for short texts like emails and about 9 for long documents. A quick check for character shingles: with 27 symbols, k = 5 gives 275 ≈ 14 million possible shingles, far more than the few thousand in one email, so chance matches are rare.

Because the windows overlap almost completely, and a rolling hash reuses the previous window's hash in O(1), while hashing from scratch re-reads all k items for every window.

A document of length L has L − k + 1 shingles. From scratch that is about L·k steps; rolling is about L steps: remove the item that leaves, add the item that enters. Example: one page of 10,000 characters with k = 50 costs about 500,000 steps from scratch and about 10,000 rolling.

At 100 million pages that is 5 × 1013 steps against 1012: the same job on 50 times fewer machines. It also makes the cost independent of k, so you can tune k freely, and it needs only O(1) extra memory per document, because no substring is ever copied.

code.title: Stress test: brute-force matcher against KMP on 1,000 random inputs

followUps:
Loop a few thousand times: make a small random text and pattern, run the slow obvious version and the fast version, and stop at the first input where the answers differ.

Random rnd = new Random(1);                 // fixed seed: failures can be repeated
for (int t = 0; t < 5000; t++) {
  String txt = randAB(rnd, 1 + rnd.nextInt(12)), pat = randAB(rnd, 1 + rnd.nextInt(3));
  if (!brute(txt, pat).equals(fast(txt, pat)))
    throw new AssertionError(txt + " / " + pat);
}

Three choices make it work: (1) a tiny alphabet such as only 'a' and 'b', so matches, overlaps and partial matches happen all the time; with 26 letters almost nothing matches and bugs stay hidden; (2) short strings, so the failing case is small enough to trace by hand, for example "aaa" / "aa" exposes a lost overlap; (3) compare full lists of positions, not just counts.

Inputs where almost the whole pattern matches at every starting position and the mismatch comes only at the last character. Then each of the N − M + 1 starts costs about M comparisons, which is O(N·M).

The classic case: text = "aaaa…a" and pattern = "aaa…ab". With N = 100,000 and M = 50,000 that is about 50,000 starts × 50,000 comparisons = 2.5 billion steps, while KMP needs at most 2N + 2M = 300,000.

Other bad shapes are the same idea: a pattern of all 'a' in a text of all 'a' (every position matches fully), and periodic strings such as "ababab…" searched for "abab…abc". Random text is not a problem, because a wrong start usually fails on the first or second character, so naive search runs in about N steps there. That is why naive matching looks fine in tests and then times out on a judge's worst case.
